WHO shall not be liable for damages arising from its use. The document includes Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome (PICO) questions to guide clinical recommendations. For example, among children and adolescents (0–18 years) who have been or may have been exposed to sexual abuse, do interventions providing enhanced adherence support for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) improve adherence or prevent HIV compared to no adherence support? Additionally, is screening and treatment for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) more effective than presumptive treatment in preventing and managing adverse outcomes such as emotional or behavioral disorders, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, or caregiver outcomes? The document also addresses existing WHO recommendations on topics such as pregnancy prevention and management (e.g., emergency contraception, safe abortion), vaccines to prevent STIs (e.g., hepatitis B, human papillomavirus), HIV prevention (e.g., PEP regimens), and mental health interventions for emotional and behavioral disorders. Good clinical practices are outlined for childand adolescent-centered, gender-sensitive, and trauma-informed care. These include obtaining medical history, conducting forensic interviews, performing physical examinations, and documenting findings in a manner that minimizes harm or trauma. The document also discusses reporting requirements, including considerations related to the age of sexual consent and statutory rape laws, as well as the values and preferences of healthcare providers, children, adolescents, and their caregivers regarding reporting sexual abuse. Ethical, safety, and human rights principles are emphasized as essential in guiding clinical practice. Additionally, good practices for providing information and education about sexual abuse to children, adolescents, and their caregivers are highlighted to promote timely access to health services.
